takeaway: A below-knee cast can compress the common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck. It supplies the anterior and lateral compartments, so dorsiflexion is lost (foot drop).

question.text: After 6 weeks in a below-knee cast for an ankle fracture, a patient develops common peroneal nerve palsy. Which statement about the examination is true?
question.say: After six weeks in a below-knee cast for an ankle fracture, a patient develops common peroneal nerve palsy. Which statement about the examination is true?

answer.text: There would be no dorsiflexion of the foot.

lines.text: The trouble starts at the top of a below-knee cast.
Here the common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck, where the cast can compress it.
This nerve supplies the anterior and lateral compartments of the leg.
They dorsiflex the foot, ankle and toes, and evert the foot.
So with a palsy there is no dorsiflexion: the foot drops.
The superficial peroneal nerve supplies most of the dorsum; the deep peroneal, the first web space.
The sole is not its territory, so sole sensation stays normal.
